appraisal_events.evidence: « Mais ils ne pensent rien du tout ; je leur ai dit que vous êtes sublime et ils sont beaucoup plus intimidés que vous. »
appraisal_events.explanation: Saint-Loup answers his friend's embarrassment by reporting that he has vouched for him in extravagant terms and that his own circle is the intimidated party, which locally raises the narrator inside that group.

appraisal_events.evidence: « C'est que je vais vous dire, on m'a assuré qu'elle me croit tout à fait idiot », immediately after Saint-Loup has said he does not even know whether she is aware of their acquaintance.
appraisal_events.explanation: The woman whose photograph he is angling for is reported to hold him a complete idiot; the verdict reaches him only at second hand and sits oddly against Saint-Loup's ignorance of what she knows.

status_effects.explanation: Saint-Loup has presented him to his regiment friends as sublime, and their reported intimidation is deference registered inside the passage's world.
Against that local credit stands the verdict of the woman he most wants to reach, who is said to think him altogether stupid.

ambiguities: The duchess's contempt is pure hearsay ('on m'a assuré') and is reported one line after Saint-Loup admits he does not know whether she knows of the narrator at all, so how far it should count as her actual judgment is left open.
